title: Why I send my kid to low-income urban public schools
gist: Yglesias argues, against reactions to Nikole Hannah-Jones's regret piece, that affluent urban parents need not flee to the suburbs or private school: his son's Title I, majority-minority D.C. elementary school was well-run and the trade-offs were minor versus tuition or moving costs. School quality in high-need areas varies a lot and depends on policy.

insights.claim: Yglesias's son attended a D.C. Title I public elementary school from pre-K through fifth grade that is 47 percent Black, 20 percent Hispanic and 22 percent English language learners, and now attends a demographically similar zoned middle school.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows that some affluent urban families stay in neighborhood public schools rather than paying for private school or moving.
insights.quote: a Title I school that is 47 percent Black, 20 percent Hispanic, and 22 percent English language learners

insights.claim: Even on purely selfish grounds, Yglesias judges the downsides of a low-income majority-minority school minor compared with private-school tuition or the hassle of moving to the suburbs.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Questions the assumption that affluent families with children must leave cities, which matters for urban housing demand and private-education demand.
insights.quote: I’d say the difficulties and downsides were minor compared with the price of private school tuition or the annoyance of moving to the suburbs
insights.locator: But our experience being the affluent

insights.claim: A critical mass of affluent, educated, engaged parents at a high-poverty school makes a real difference to teachers and students, so middle-class participation has positive spillovers.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Supports the idea that keeping middle-class families in cities can improve urban school quality over time.
insights.quote: the presence of a critical mass of affluent, educated, engaged parents I think made a real difference in the lives of the teachers and the students

insights.claim: Exposure to a broader socioeconomic mix helped his child learn to handle a wider range of social interactions than an affluent-only school would have.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A non-academic benefit that affects how families value school choice.
insights.locator: What’s more, not only do I

insights.claim: Schools serving high-need populations vary widely in quality, and policy matters: not every school with unfavorable demographics is dysfunctional, so parents should look at their local specifics rather than assume.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Demographic averages are a poor guide to school quality, and that affects neighborhood valuations.
insights.quote: Not every school with unfavorable demographics is a dysfunctional mess — policy matters!

insights.claim: Yglesias warns it would be a shame if every affluent urban parent of a toddler decided to flee to the suburbs, implying a risk of middle-class flight from cities driven by blanket skepticism of inner-city schools.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Family out-migration from cities affects urban rents, suburban home demand and municipal tax bases.
insights.quote: it would be a shame if every affluent urban parent of a toddler decides they need to flee to the suburbs

insights.claim: Among Yglesias's acquaintances, especially non-parents, the main takeaway from Hannah-Jones's piece was that parents must fully optimize for their own child, a sign that elite sentiment is moving away from public-school idealism.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shifting elite attitudes toward school choice could raise private-school and suburban demand.

insights.claim: D.C. offers universal public pre-K starting at age three.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Free pre-K lowers the cost of raising young children in D.C. and may keep families in the city.
